questions.question: What is an Observable, and how is it different from a Promise?

definition.text: Observables model subscribed streams; promises represent one eventual outcome.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Promise-based APIs represent one eventual resolution or rejection, but UIs also need multiple values over time: input changes, WebSocket events, timers and request flows. RxJS Observables provide a common composable protocol for these streams. Angular HttpClient returns Observables so consumers can transform responses and control subscriptions.
motivation.historicalNote: Promises and Observables solve overlapping, not identical, problems. Observables are not automatically faster or inherently asynchronous: an Observable can emit synchronously, and work starts according to how its producer was implemented.

problemSolved.before: A shipment screen combines ad hoc callbacks, timers and one-shot promises, making cleanup and transformation inconsistent.
problemSolved.after: The screen uses Observables with explicit subscription semantics, operators, and teardown where appropriate; one-shot async tasks may still use Promises.
benefits: Supports zero, one or many next values followed by completion or error
Composable filtering, transformation and flattening operators
Explicit teardown via unsubscribe for streams that need it
Works with Angular AsyncPipe and RxJS interop

characteristics: An Observable is a recipe for notifications: next, error and complete; terminal signals end a subscription.
Many sources are cold: each subscription triggers independent producer work, but hot streams can share sources.
Emission may be synchronous or asynchronous; Observable is not synonymous with asynchronous execution.
Unsubscribing tears down its subscription but cannot automatically undo external side effects already committed.
A Promise settles once and remains eager after its producer starts; cancelling a subscriber does not turn it into a cancellable Promise.

simpleAnalogy.title: Radio channel versus delivered parcel
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A parcel arrives once and is either delivered or fails, like a Promise. A radio subscription may deliver many broadcasts until you disconnect; listeners do not cause the station to repeat yesterday’s news.

industryExample.scenario: A shipment dashboard loads initial shipment details and then updates live delivery progress.
industryExample.implementation: Use an HttpClient Observable for the one-time details request and a separate shared transport stream for live status updates. Render current state via AsyncPipe or a signal, and dispose the live subscription when its scope ends.
industryExample.businessImpact: Users see both initial details and subsequent changes without writing nested event callbacks.
industryExample.importantConstraint: The backend owns authoritative shipment state; receiving a message or cancelling a stream never guarantees a delivery event was rolled back.

useCases: HttpClient response pipelines and declarative templates
Search-input changes and form valueChanges streams
WebSocket tracking or notifications
Timer, user event and retryable asynchronous workflows

steps: Component creates a typed cold Observable for a simulated shipment lookup
No producer runs merely because the Observable variable exists
The first subscriber triggers the producer and receives one result
A second subscriber triggers its own execution on this cold source
An independent live stream may emit multiple statuses until teardown

diagrams.title: Observables and Promises: end-to-end flow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    actor U as User
    participant C as Angular Screen
    participant O as Cold Observable
    participant P as Producer
    U->>C: Open shipment
    C->>O: subscribe()
    O->>P: Start simulated lookup
    P-->>O: next(shipment)
    O-->>C: value
    P-->>O: complete()
    C-->>U: Show details
diagrams.caption: Educational example; domain authorization and persisted system state remain server responsibilities.

codeExample.runtime: RxJS 7+ with TypeScript; run with npx tsx in a project with rxjs installed.
explanation: The Observable producer increments executions only after subscription, showing cold execution.
Two subscriptions execute this producer twice; not all Observables are cold, so do not generalize to every source.
firstValueFrom bridges a stream to a Promise; it is appropriate only when an emission is expected.
A hanging Observable that never emits or completes can leave firstValueFrom pending; use timeout or take(1) where appropriate.

projectExperience.example: I would use a cold HttpClient stream for initial shipment details and a separately managed live tracking stream. I would demonstrate distinct subscriptions, cancellation and teardown in the practice project.
evidenceToCollect: A screen showing initial fetch and live updates separately
A test proving cold-source subscription count
A screenshot or recording proving live stream cleanup after navigation
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed learning-project narrative. Do not claim it is deployed, used by customers, or previously implemented unless evidence exists.

pitfalls: Subscribing to a cold HttpClient Observable twice can issue duplicate requests.
Unsubscribing from a client-side request cannot revoke a server-side write that already committed.
A never-ending Observable passed to lastValueFrom may leave the Promise unresolved.
Subscribing imperatively without teardown can leak long-lived streams.
whenNotToUse: Do not choose Observables for a simple synchronous calculation with no event stream.
Do not claim all Observables are lazy, cold, asynchronous or inherently cancellable at the business layer.
Do not use Promise conversion for a stream when ongoing emissions are required.

alternatives.name: Promise/async-await
alternatives.bestFor: Single asynchronous value and naturally sequential control flow
alternatives.tradeoff: Cannot represent multiple future values; producer cancellation requires separate design

alternatives.name: Signal
alternatives.bestFor: Current reactive UI state with synchronous reads
alternatives.tradeoff: Not inherently an event/history stream or request cancellation primitive

alternatives.name: EventTarget/callback
alternatives.bestFor: Small local event source with few transformations
alternatives.tradeoff: Manual composition and cleanup can become complex

testing.strategy: Run the sample in the declared runtime, write behavioral assertions using fake time or controlled test streams when relevant, and distinguish syntax checks from Angular template compilation and browser execution.

testCases.expected: Two subscriptions execute the producer twice.
An Observable error reaches the error observer and terminates that subscription.
firstValueFrom resolves with the first emitted value.

negativeCases: Test a never-emitting source with timeout rather than allowing a hanging test.
Confirm server writes cannot be assumed rolled back after client unsubscribe.

beginner: What do next, error and complete represent?
intermediate: How do hot and cold sources change multicasting behavior?
advanced: How would you cache a GET response without introducing stale-user data?
expert: How would you reason about subscription ownership and server side effects in cross-region event delivery?

answer.finalTakeaway: Use Observables for composable streams; choose Promises for single outcomes and model teardown explicitly.

learningOutcomes: Explain observables and promises clearly and distinguish related APIs.

Identify a production anti-pattern and propose a safer alternative.

questions.question: What are Subject and BehaviorSubject, and when would you use each?

definition.text: Subjects multicast notifications; BehaviorSubjects additionally retain current values.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Ordinary cold Observables often repeat their producer for each subscriber. Sometimes many UI consumers must receive events from one shared source. Subject is an observer and Observable, allowing explicit multicasting. BehaviorSubject extends that model with an initial/current value for late subscribers.
motivation.historicalNote: BehaviorSubject is an RxJS construct, not a built-in Angular state store. Its current-value behavior can be valuable, but it does not automatically provide immutable state, authorization or persistence.

problemSolved.before: A workspace header and permissions panel invent separate event callbacks and fall out of sync after workspace selection.
problemSolved.after: A focused service exposes a read-only Observable of active workspace state, backed by a private BehaviorSubject seeded with a valid initial state.
benefits: Multicasts pushed values to multiple active subscribers
BehaviorSubject provides a current value immediately on normal subscription
Encapsulation protects writes by exposing asObservable()
Simple migration path for an existing RxJS-driven service

characteristics: Subject has no required initial value and does not replay earlier next notifications to late subscribers.
BehaviorSubject requires an initial value and supplies its current value on subscription while active.
Both are hot multicast sources whose next() can be invoked by producers.
An error or completion terminates a Subject; a terminal BehaviorSubject should not be treated as a perpetual reusable store.
Exposing asObservable() prevents consumers from calling next() through the public API.

simpleAnalogy.title: Town announcement versus current noticeboard
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A public announcement is heard only by people already listening (Subject). A noticeboard shows the current instruction to a newcomer immediately (BehaviorSubject). Neither is automatically an archival log.

industryExample.scenario: Users switch between tenant workspaces and several components must reflect the active workspace.
industryExample.implementation: A WorkspaceService owns a private BehaviorSubject seeded with null, exposes an observable to the header and navigation, and explicitly clears tenant-specific resources on switching.
industryExample.businessImpact: Existing and newly mounted UI areas agree on which workspace is selected.
industryExample.importantConstraint: The server still validates tenant membership on every relevant request. A client-side BehaviorSubject cannot enforce tenant isolation or protect against stale in-flight responses.

useCases: Current active tenant or workspace state in an RxJS-heavy app
One-to-many in-process notification bus for ephemeral events
Form wizard state scoped to a route and seeded predictably
Broadcasting selected filters to multiple widgets

steps: Workspace service creates BehaviorSubject with null initial value
Header subscribes and immediately receives null
User selects a permitted demo workspace; service calls next()
Header and menu receive the same new workspace
A late subscriber immediately receives the current workspace
Logout or tenant transition resets sensitive scoped state

diagrams.title: Subject and BehaviorSubject: end-to-end flow
diagrams.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    actor U as User
    participant W as WorkspaceService
    participant H as Header Subscriber
    participant M as Menu Subscriber
    H->>W: subscribe()
    W-->>H: null (initial)
    U->>W: selectWorkspace(DEMO-A)
    W-->>H: DEMO-A
    M->>W: subscribe()
    W-->>M: DEMO-A (current)
diagrams.caption: Educational example; domain authorization and persisted system state remain server responsibilities.

codeExample.runtime: RxJS 7+ with TypeScript; run with npx tsx in a project with rxjs installed.
explanation: BehaviorSubject starts with null, avoiding a made-up default tenant.
The first subscriber receives null and then DEMO-A; the late subscriber immediately receives DEMO-A.
Only the service can call next() because the subject is private.
snapshot() is a convenience read of current state, not an authorization check or persistence guarantee.

projectExperience.example: I would implement WorkspaceState in the SaaS practice app, subscribe from a header and a menu, and test the initial value and late-subscription behavior.
evidenceToCollect: A test showing the initial null emission and current-value delivery
A logout test ensuring tenant-specific data gets cleared
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed learning-project narrative. Do not claim it is deployed, used by customers, or previously implemented unless evidence exists.

pitfalls: Late subscribers to plain Subject do not receive previous events.
BehaviorSubject needs a meaningful initial value; using a fake real tenant can be dangerous.
Using a root-scoped BehaviorSubject for sensitive user/tenant state without clearing it can expose stale information.
BehaviorSubject does not automatically deduplicate equal values.
A terminal or errored subject is not appropriate as a long-lived reinitializable store.
whenNotToUse: Do not use a global Subject as a substitute for typed domain contracts.
Do not rely on client-side current workspace state for backend tenant authorization.
Do not expose the writable Subject publicly when consumers should only observe it.

alternatives.name: Subject
alternatives.bestFor: Transient notifications where late subscribers should not replay

alternatives.name: ReplaySubject(1)
alternatives.bestFor: Replay latest emission without requiring an initial seed
alternatives.tradeoff: No initial synchronous state before first emission

alternatives.name: Angular signal
alternatives.bestFor: Synchronous current UI state with derived computations
alternatives.tradeoff: No built-in stream semantics; use RxJS for async pipelines

testing.strategy: Run the sample in the declared runtime, write behavioral assertions using fake time or controlled test streams when relevant, and distinguish syntax checks from Angular template compilation and browser execution.

testCases.expected: First BehaviorSubject subscriber immediately receives null.
Subscriber added after selecting DEMO-A immediately receives DEMO-A.
Only service exposes select(); consumer cannot call next() on selected$.

negativeCases: Test state clearing after logout or workspace change.
Confirm Subject late subscriber sees no prior next value.

beginner: Why does BehaviorSubject need an initial value?
intermediate: How do ReplaySubject(1) and BehaviorSubject differ before the first value?
advanced: How would you prevent stale in-flight tenant requests from contaminating state?
expert: What controls prevent cross-tenant state leakage through shared caches or SSR?

answer.finalTakeaway: Choose Subject for events and BehaviorSubject for current values; neither substitutes for server authorization.

questions.question: What are subscribe(), pipe(), map(), filter() and tap() in RxJS?

definition.text: RxJS operators transform streams; subscriptions activate observable consumption paths.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Without composition, data preparation is spread across nested subscribe callbacks, making transformations difficult to reuse and test. RxJS pipe chains declaratively transform or observe values before a consumer subscribes.
motivation.historicalNote: pipe() does not start a cold producer by itself. Operators such as map and filter are pure transformation/selectors when their supplied callbacks are pure; tap is intended for side effects like diagnostics.

problemSolved.before: An orders screen subscribes to raw rows and mixes filtering, mapping, logging and display assignment in one callback.
problemSolved.after: A typed Observable pipeline filters paid orders, maps them to display labels, uses tap for optional instrumentation and leaves the final subscriber to consume the view models.
benefits: Readable, composable stream transformations
Separated pure mapping from effects
Simple testing of output values
Reuse of operator chains across domain features

characteristics: subscribe() attaches a consumer; cold producers typically start then and can be torn down by unsubscribe().
pipe() returns a new Observable description; it does not mutate the original source.
map() transforms each next value one-for-one, while filter() suppresses next values whose predicate is false.
tap() observes values or notifications but normally passes the same values through; an exception inside tap can error the stream.
Operator order matters: map before filter may change predicate inputs and behavior.

simpleAnalogy.title: Mail sorting conveyor
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A sorting line rejects nonpriority envelopes (filter), adds standardized labels to accepted envelopes (map), and records a scan (tap). Opening the receiving desk connects the consumer (subscribe).

industryExample.scenario: An operations screen displays only paid orders with readable currency labels.
industryExample.implementation: Represent incoming order events as a typed source, filter to paid orders, project to labels, and log processing in a tap callback; subscribe for display or use AsyncPipe in Angular.
industryExample.businessImpact: Order widgets display consistent derived information with a pipeline that can be unit tested.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Never rely on frontend filtering as proof of payment or authorization; payment state must be confirmed by the backend.

useCases: Convert backend DTOs to Angular view models
Exclude unwanted event notifications
Log or measure pipeline processing without changing values
Transform form and search streams before UI rendering

steps: An order stream emits paid, pending and paid records
filter() excludes the pending order
map() creates a read-only formatted output for paid records
tap() records a diagnostic message but leaves values unchanged
The subscriber renders only the two paid order labels

diagrams.title: Core RxJS operators: end-to-end flow
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
    A[Order source] --> B{filter paid?}
    B -- No --> X[Suppress emission]
    B -- Yes --> C[map to label]
    C --> D[tap diagnostic]
    D --> E[Subscriber]
diagrams.caption: Educational example; domain authorization and persisted system state remain server responsibilities.

codeExample.runtime: RxJS 7+ with TypeScript; run with npx tsx in a project with rxjs installed.
explanation: from(orders) emits each array item as a separate notification.
filter checks the typed status property, map converts each accepted order into a label.
tap logs observable output without intentionally modifying its emitted value.
A subscription activates this cold pipeline. In Angular, prefer AsyncPipe for template-bound streams when feasible.

projectExperience.example: I would use a pipeline like this for the E-Commerce order list and write a marble-independent unit test using toArray() to assert exact displayed labels.
evidenceToCollect: A captured test confirming only paid orders are shown
A code review demonstrating no nested subscribe for basic transformations
A note explaining why server-side order authorization remains mandatory
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed learning-project narrative. Do not claim it is deployed, used by customers, or previously implemented unless evidence exists.

pitfalls: Calling subscribe() separately in several consumers may repeat cold HTTP requests.
Returning a value from tap does not replace the emitted value; use map instead.
Mutating objects inside map or tap can create surprising shared-state behavior.
filter only suppresses emissions; it does not remove entries from an array inside one emission unless you map that array.
whenNotToUse: Do not use tap to transform values that downstream consumers depend upon.
Do not put long business workflows or writes inside arbitrary logging tap callbacks.
Do not use client-side filter for access control or financial truth.

alternatives.name: Native array map/filter
alternatives.tradeoff: Not a stream of values over time

alternatives.name: computed() signal
alternatives.bestFor: Derived state from synchronous reactive sources
alternatives.tradeoff: Not a replacement for event-stream operators

alternatives.name: Imperative subscribe handler
alternatives.tradeoff: Transformation and effects become tangled with rendering

testing.strategy: Run the sample in the declared runtime, write behavioral assertions using fake time or controlled test streams when relevant, and distinguish syntax checks from Angular template compilation and browser execution.

testCases.expected: Only paid order records reach subscriber.
Output labels contain order IDs and minor-unit values.
Downstream values are unchanged by diagnostic tap.

negativeCases: Check changing operator order does not silently alter the business result.

intermediate: Why are nested subscriptions difficult to maintain?
advanced: When would switchMap or concatMap replace a manual nested subscribe?
expert: How would you ensure a complex shared pipeline does not duplicate writes when subscribers increase?

answer.finalTakeaway: Prefer declarative pipelines: filter selects, map transforms, tap observes, and subscription consumes.

questions.question: What are Angular Signals? Explain signal(), computed(), and how they differ from Observables.

definition.text: Signals hold reactive values; computed signals derive cached results.

motivation.whyIntroduced: Angular components frequently need a synchronous, readable current value with automatic UI invalidation. Signals provide fine-grained reactive state tracking and memoized derivations without requiring every local state read to be subscribed to as an asynchronous event stream.
motivation.historicalNote: Angular Signals were introduced in modern Angular and are complementary to RxJS. An Observable can represent a temporal sequence of notifications, while a Signal always represents a current value read by calling it. Angular provides toSignal/toObservable interop.

problemSolved.before: A dashboard stores subtotal and tax in separately maintained variables, which can drift when the cart changes.
problemSolved.after: Store cart items in a writable signal and compute subtotal and item count from that source; Angular tracks the dependencies of rendered computed values.
benefits: Synchronous access to current state
Memoized and lazy derived computations
Automatic dependency tracking during reactive reads
Straightforward rendering in Angular templates

characteristics: A writable signal is read by invoking it and updated with set() or update().
computed() returns a read-only, lazily evaluated, memoized Signal whose dependencies are tracked dynamically.
Signals compare values with Object.is by default unless a different equality is configured; deep object mutation is not automatically detected.
Effects are intended mainly for synchronizing with imperative APIs, not for copying one signal into another.
Signals and RxJS interoperate, but Signals do not natively model each event in a time-ordered async stream.

simpleAnalogy.title: Thermostat and derived comfort indicator
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A thermostat shows the current temperature (signal), and a calculated comfort category depends on that reading (computed). An event log records every temperature change over time (Observable-like stream).

industryExample.scenario: A shopping cart must display a current item count and subtotal while users change quantities.
industryExample.implementation: Keep line items in a signal and derive the count and subtotal with computed. Use a backend API for price and inventory validation at checkout, not the client subtotal as financial authority.
industryExample.businessImpact: Cart summaries stay internally consistent without manual synchronization of multiple derived fields.
industryExample.importantConstraint: Currency values should be represented in minor units or an appropriate decimal model; frontend totals are previews, not authoritative checkout pricing.

useCases: Local component state and template reactivity
Derived counts, sums and selected-tab labels
Feature state exposed as read-only signals
Bridging a subscription stream to view state via toSignal()

steps: Component creates a writable items signal
Template reads itemCount() and subtotalMinor() computed signals
User adds another line item using update() with a new array reference
Angular invalidates dependent computed caches
Next template read re-evaluates computed values and renders new totals

diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart TD
    A[User changes quantity] --> B[items.update creates new array]
    B --> C[Writable items signal]
    C --> D[computed itemCount]
    C --> E[computed subtotalMinor]
    D --> F[Angular template]
    E --> F
diagrams.caption: Educational example; domain authorization and persisted system state remain server responsibilities.

codeExample.runtime: Angular 17+ standalone component; requires @angular/core, @angular/forms and rxjs in an Angular workspace.
explanation: items is a writable Signal containing immutable-in-practice line items.
itemCount and subtotalMinor are computed; their functions only read state and calculate derived values.
addOne creates new object and array references instead of mutating the array in place.
The template reads signals with parentheses. A real checkout must revalidate every price and available quantity on the server.

projectExperience.example: I would implement the E-Commerce cart summary with signals and add tests proving displayed counts and totals change after quantity updates.
evidenceToCollect: A working cart component screenshot before/after click
A unit test checking subtotal changes from 1250 to 2500 minor units
A server-side checkout test demonstrating client prices are not trusted
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed learning-project narrative. Do not claim it is deployed, used by customers, or previously implemented unless evidence exists.

pitfalls: Mutating an array or object held by a signal without set/update may not trigger consumers.
Computed values are not writable; try updating their source signals instead.
Using effect() to propagate derived state can produce cycles or unnecessary work.
Signals hold latest state; they do not preserve every intermediate change as an event log.
Repeated toSignal() calls can create repeated subscriptions; create once and reuse.
whenNotToUse: Do not use a Signal to replace all RxJS event streams and HTTP orchestration by default.
Do not use effect to mirror another signal when computed directly represents the derivation.
Do not treat client-side subtotal as authoritative order pricing.

alternatives.bestFor: Existing RxJS service needing both current value and multicasting
alternatives.tradeoff: Requires subscriptions or interop to read in templates conveniently

alternatives.name: Observable pipeline
alternatives.bestFor: Cancellation, events over time and async composition
alternatives.tradeoff: Does not inherently expose synchronous current value

alternatives.name: Ordinary component field
alternatives.bestFor: Nonreactive fixed configuration or simple local data

Assert pricing is revalidated on the backend before order acceptance.

expert: How would you structure Signals and RxJS in an SSR-safe, tenant-aware state boundary?

answer.finalTakeaway: Use Signals for reactive current state and computed derivations; keep RxJS for event-stream orchestration.

questions.question: Implement a search input using debounceTime, distinctUntilChanged and switchMap.

definition.text: Debounced search waits, ignores repeats, and switches requests safely.

motivation.whyIntroduced: A request on every keystroke overloads search APIs and can render results for stale queries. Debouncing limits bursts, distinctUntilChanged avoids consecutive duplicate search terms, and switchMap switches to the newest inner Observable so previous response emissions cannot overwrite newer results.
motivation.historicalNote: switchMap unsubscribes from the previous inner subscription when a new source value arrives. HttpClient may abort an in-flight request on unsubscribe, but cancellation is not a guarantee that server work or already-committed effects are undone.

problemSolved.before: Typing B, BO, BOO triggers three requests, and a slow response for B can overwrite fresh results for BOO.
problemSolved.after: Normalize input, wait 300ms of inactivity, ignore repeated queries, and switch the latest query to a typed read-only product search request.
benefits: Limits request frequency during typing bursts
Avoids consecutive duplicate searches
Prevents older subscribed results from overwriting latest search output
Makes loading, error and empty-result behavior explicit

characteristics: debounceTime(300) emits after a 300ms period without another source emission.
distinctUntilChanged() compares consecutive emitted values with strict equality by default.
switchMap() unsubscribes from the previous inner Observable when a newer query arrives.
catchError inside switchMap preserves the outer input stream after a failed request.
takeUntilDestroyed() or AsyncPipe scopes subscription lifetime; cancellation never guarantees server-side side-effect reversal.

simpleAnalogy.title: Librarian answering a changing request
simpleAnalogy.explanation: A librarian waits until you finish spelling a book title, ignores the same title repeated, and stops preparing an older answer when you ask about a newer title.

industryExample.scenario: A shopper searches products while typing quickly on a retail storefront.
industryExample.implementation: Bind a non-nullable FormControl to the input, trim and lowercase terms, debounce, skip duplicates, and use switchMap to query an API. A mock Observable backend demonstrates success and error responses without needing a running server.
industryExample.businessImpact: Fewer wasted read requests and consistent latest-query results improve catalog usability.
industryExample.importantConstraint: The server must separately enforce query limits, input validation, search authorization where applicable, and pagination. Do not use switchMap for non-idempotent writes such as payment submission.

useCases: Product catalogs with autocomplete
Shipment finder with status term search
Clinician directory search on approved data
Search-as-you-type admin tables

steps: User types several characters into a reactive FormControl
valueChanges emits input strings
map normalizes whitespace and case
debounceTime waits for an idle interval and distinctUntilChanged skips repeats
switchMap begins newest search and unsubscribes from previous search
Result Observable emits matching products or a handled error-state fallback
AsyncPipe updates the Angular template and unsubscribes on teardown

diagrams.title: Debounced search with RxJS: end-to-end flow

sequenceDiagram
    actor U as Shopper
    participant F as Angular FormControl
    participant O as RxJS Pipeline
    participant A as Search API
    participant V as Results UI
    U->>F: Type b
    U->>F: Type bo
    U->>F: Type book
    F->>O: valueChanges events

    U->>F: Type books
    O-->>A: Unsubscribe previous observable
    O->>A: search(books)
    A-->>O: latest matches
    O-->>V: display latest results
diagrams.caption: Educational example; domain authorization and persisted system state remain server responsibilities.

codeExample.runtime: Angular 17+ standalone component; requires @angular/core, @angular/forms and rxjs in an Angular workspace.
explanation: The input is bound to a non-nullable FormControl so valueChanges emits strings.
startWith seeds an initial query; debounceTime applies to the initial emission too.
map normalizes before distinctUntilChanged so differences in case/space do not trigger duplicate searches.
switchMap ensures that only results from the latest active inner subscription reach the template.
The sample mock emits synchronously when subscribed; replace it with typed HttpClient calls for an actual network-backed demo.
catchError is inside switchMap, keeping subsequent keystrokes usable after one request fails; the sample renders an empty list on error.

projectExperience.example: I would implement this search feature in the E-Commerce practice project, then replace the mock with HttpClient and test stale-response prevention using controlled request delays.
evidenceToCollect: A demo showing search normalization and debouncing
An HttpTestingController test proving old requests are cancelled/ignored
A component test showing empty-state rendering and recovery after a failed request
projectExperience.doNotClaim: This is a proposed learning-project narrative. Do not claim it is deployed, used by customers, or previously implemented unless evidence exists.

pitfalls: Without debouncing, every keystroke can trigger costly requests.
Putting catchError outside switchMap can terminate the whole input search stream after an error.
switchMap is often inappropriate for writes; unsubscribing a submitted payment request does not undo the payment.
The mock data search can hide issues such as server pagination, latency and rate limits.
AsyncPipe cleans up the template subscription, but shared service streams may still require explicit lifecycle ownership.
whenNotToUse: Never use switchMap for payment, order creation or other writes that must not be silently superseded.
Do not trust client-side search filtering to enforce sensitive-data permissions.
Do not add debounce to every action; button submissions may need immediate handling and distinct coordination.

alternatives.name: concatMap
alternatives.bestFor: Writes that must be serialized in order
alternatives.tradeoff: Later work waits behind earlier work

alternatives.name: exhaustMap
alternatives.bestFor: Ignore subsequent triggers while one operation runs

alternatives.name: mergeMap
alternatives.tradeoff: Responses may arrive out of order

alternatives.name: Signal plus toObservable
alternatives.bestFor: Signal-driven search input with RxJS request pipeline

testing.strategy: Run the sample in the declared runtime, write behavioral assertions using fake time or controlled test streams when relevant, and distinguish syntax checks from Angular template compilation and browser execution.

testCases.expected: Only one search happens for rapid typing within 300ms.
"Book" followed by " book " does not retrigger the same normalized term.
A late response from an obsolete search never replaces the latest results.
A failed API search still allows a later valid search.
